title: Being with the dying
hookLine: presence, prayer and quiet at a bedside
tomorrow: why lay a white cloth over the coffin at a Catholic funeral?

cards: A bedside has its own sounds: a machine humming, a cart going by in the hall, someone else's TV through the wall. And beside someone who is dying, the hardest sound can be the silence. What do you say?
Maybe nothing much. The Catholic answer is older and simpler than a speech: stay.

teach.b: On his last night, in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus doesn't ask his friends for advice. He asks for company, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death; stay you here, and watch."
They fall asleep, and he comes back and asks again.

teach.h: HIS MOTHER STOOD BY THE CROSS.
teach.b: The next day, John writes: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother." No speech is recorded from her there. She stands.
Here's one to tell a friend: an old Latin hymn about that moment is named for her posture, Stabat Mater, the mother was standing. At a Catholic bedside, staying looks plain.

teach.h: A HAND, A ROSARY, THE QUIET.
teach.b: A hand held. A wet cloth on dry lips.
A rosary said softly, or just the end of the Hail Mary, over and over. A call to the priest, if it hasn't happened. And quiet, without hurrying to fill it.
The Church has its own prayers for this hour, commending the person to God as they go. But the first gift needs no words at all. You don't have to fix anything.

how: Catholics keep vigil with the dying at home or in the hospital, praying the rosary or the Hail Mary, calling a priest for the anointing and viaticum, and using the Church's prayers of commendation for the dying.

games.q: what does “being with the dying” mean?
o: staying with someone at the end, without fixing
telling a dying person all you never said
keeping a dying person busy and distracted

p: now and at the hour of our death

s: in Gethsemane, Jesus asked his friends for advice
he asked them to stay and watch.
John says Jesus's mother stood by the cross
now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother.
beside someone dying, you should keep talking so it's never silent
quiet presence is the gift. you don't have to fix anything.

games.q: your friend's grandfather is dying three states away, and she can't get there in time. she feels useless. what fits today's lesson?
o: a video call: hold the phone near him, pray, or just stay on.
nothing; being with the dying only counts in the room.
a long letter covering everything she never said to him.
games.why: Jesus asked his friends to stay and watch; presence is the gift, even through a screen. stay beside.

practice: Learn one line by heart now, so it's there when you need it: the end of the Hail Mary, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Say it slowly, out loud, three times.
Then sit with the name of someone you'd want to say it beside.

wordCard.voice: Being with the dying. Presence, prayer and quiet at a bedside, staying when there's nothing left to fix.

orig.note: Latin: the sorrowful mother was standing. the opening of an old hymn about Mary at the cross.

carryVoice: Your line: stay beside, the way Mary stood by the cross and simply stayed. Good night.

sources.q: My soul is sorrowful even unto death; stay you here, and watch.
